summary: Defines a new BGP Outbound Route Filter type, the Address Prefix ORF, for filtering routes by address prefix. It supports matching by prefix length or range, wildcards, and exact prefixes across address families. A router can use it to tell a peer which routes it wants to receive.

eli5.summary: It is a wish list sent to a neighbor router: only send me addresses that look like this. The neighbor skips everything else, which saves time and effort for both.

questions: what is bgp address prefix orf
how does bgp orf first match work
subtitle: A BGP filter type that lets a router ask its neighbor to send only routes whose address prefixes match a list.

tldr.problem: A BGP speaker may want its peer to skip routes it does not need, and the filter needs a way to say which address prefixes to accept or reject.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Address Prefix ORF, ORF-type 64. Each entry holds a sequence number, a permit or deny, a prefix, and optional minimum and maximum prefix lengths, and the first matching entry decides.
tldr.outcome: A router can push precise address-prefix filtering to its peer, covering exact, length-range and wild-card matches, with no new security issues.

today: RFC 5292 is a Proposed Standard from August 2008. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Outbound Route Filtering capability of RFC 5291 lets a BGP speaker send its peer a set of Outbound Route Filters (ORFs). The peer uses them to filter the routing updates it sends back. RFC 5292 adds a new ORF type, the Address Prefix ORF, which filters on address prefixes.

It supports matching by prefix length or length range, wild-card matching, and exact prefix matching, for the address families of Multiprotocol BGP (RFC 4760).
sections.eli5: One router hands its neighbor a list of the kinds of addresses it wants to hear about. The neighbor then stays quiet about the rest.

sections.title: The Address Prefix ORF Entry
sections.content:
An entry has six conceptual fields: Sequence, Match, Length, Prefix, Minlen and Maxlen.

  • Sequence orders this entry among all the Address Prefix ORF entries.
  • Match is PERMIT (0) or DENY (1).
  • Length is the prefix length in bits. Zero means a prefix that matches all addresses of the family.
  • Prefix is the address prefix.
  • Minlen and Maxlen are the smallest and largest prefix lengths, in bits, that count as a match. A value of 0 means unspecified.

The values are required to satisfy 0 <= Length < Minlen <= Maxlen, but a test is skipped when its field is unspecified. Maxlen must be no more than the length in bits of a host address for the address family.
sections.eli5: Each line of the wish list says yes or no, which addresses it is about, and optionally how long or short the address pattern may be.

sections.title: Encoding
sections.content:
The ORF-type value for the Address Prefix ORF is 64. The Match field goes in the common part defined by RFC 5291. The other fields go in the type-specific part, in this order: Sequence (4 octets), Minlen (1 octet), Maxlen (1 octet), Length (1 octet), then Prefix with variable length.

The prefix is followed by enough trailing bits to end on an octet boundary, and the value of those trailing bits is irrelevant.
sections.eli5: Each wish-list line is written in a fixed order of boxes, and the last box is padded so it fills whole bytes.

sections.title: Matching Rules
sections.content:
These rules add to the general matching rules of RFC 5291. A route has NLRI in the form <Prefix, Length>. If the NLRI is neither more specific than nor equal to the entry's <Prefix, Length>, it is not a match. Otherwise the length rule in the table applies.

When several entries match, the first-match rule applies. The entry with the smallest sequence number is the sole match and decides whether the route is advertised. How the sender assigns sequence numbers is a local matter.
sections.eli5: The neighbor reads the list from the top. The first line that fits an address decides if it is sent.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document specifies a new ORF type, the Address Prefix ORF, with ORF-type value 64.

On the security side, the RFC states that the extension does not change the underlying security issues of BGP-4 (RFC 4271).
sections.eli5: The number 64 is reserved for this kind of list, and it adds no new safety worries.

items.desc: Length of the prefix in bits.

items.label: Prefix
items.desc: Address prefix, padded to an octet boundary.
